audited.caution: The repo copy is titled 'When Fear Starts Rewriting What You Believe' (track: doubt). The shelf title is 'When Fear Rewrites Theology' with the blurb 'How sincere Christians justified what they never thought they would.' and the slug is listed in client/src/lib/substackImport.ts. The live database essay at this slug is very likely a different text (the Substack chapter). The repo copy was audited; the live one was not.

audited.key: essays[] entry with n = 11, field body

scope.note: The live site serves these essays from the database. Fixing the repo copies does not change the live page unless the database row is updated too (admin or a reseed James approves).

findings.quote: The elders did not ask for a tyrant. That is the part everyone misses.
findings.replacement: The elders did not ask for a tyrant.
findings.why: The second sentence tells the reader the point is coming. He would just make the point.

findings.quote: They wanted, above all, to be like everyone else — to have what the strong nations around them had, so they would stop feeling so exposed.
findings.replacement: Above all they wanted to be like everyone else, to have what the strong nations around them had, so they'd stop feeling so exposed.
findings.why: Em-dash as the clause connector; the essay has about twenty-five.

findings.quote: It arrives as common sense. It arrives as safety. It arrives as the perfectly sane request of people who have looked at the threats around them and decided they can no longer afford to trust an invisible God to fight visible battles.
findings.replacement: It arrives as common sense and as safety, the perfectly sane request of people who have looked at the threats around them and decided they can no longer afford to trust an invisible God to fight visible battles.
findings.why: Three 'It arrives as' in a row straight after 'never arrives announced' is a drumbeat, and the same device returns four more times in the essay.

findings.quote: *You are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations* (1 Samuel 8:5).
findings.replacement: *Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations* (1 Samuel 8:5).
findings.why: Site rule is ESV verbatim. Applier: check against the repo's Bible text before landing.

findings.tell: Scripture condensed but set as quotation
findings.quote: *He will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots. He will take your daughters. He will take the best of your fields and your vineyards and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain and your flocks. And you shall be his slaves. In that day you will cry out because of your king whom you have chosen, but the Lord will not answer you in that day* (1 Samuel 8:11–18).
findings.replacement: He will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots. He will take your daughters. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain and your flocks, and you shall be his slaves (1 Samuel 8:11–17). *And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day* (1 Samuel 8:18).
findings.why: Eight verses are compressed into one italic block that reads as a quotation. Paraphrase is offered as paraphrase; the verse that is quoted is quoted whole. Applier: check verse 18 against the ESV.

findings.tell: imperative signpost; literary word for a plain one
findings.quote: Read the verb. *He will take.* Six times, *he will take.* The king is defined by extraction.
findings.replacement: The verb is *he will take*, six times over. The king is defined by what he takes.
findings.why: 'Read the verb', 'Read what the third temptation actually is', 'Read the logic' form a stamped motif. 'Extraction' is an essay word where he would say 'what he takes'.

findings.tell: rulebook leakage; em-dash; Scripture not verbatim
findings.quote: They hear the entire indictment — the conscription, the confiscation, the slavery — and they say: *No, but there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may go out before us and fight our battles* (1 Samuel 8:19–20).
findings.replacement: They hear all of it, the conscription, the confiscation, the slavery, and they say: *No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles* (1 Samuel 8:19–20).
findings.why: 'Indictment' is the brief's own vocabulary leaking into the prose. The verse drops 'may judge us and' and changes the ESV's 'No!'. The exclamation is allowed here because it is inside quoted Scripture.

findings.tell: paragraph ends by restating itself as a bold slogan
findings.quote: **Fear hears "he will fight your battles" and never finishes the sentence that says "and you shall be his slaves."**
findings.why: The paragraph has already said 'Fear hears he will fight your battles and stops listening' and 'The promise of a fighter drowns out the warning of a tyrant'. The bold line says it a third time for the screenshot.

findings.quote: Walter Brueggemann gave this whole dynamic a name that should be carved over the door of every church flirting with it. In *The Prophetic Imagination* (1978) he calls it the "royal consciousness" — the settled state of a people
findings.replacement: Walter Brueggemann gave this a name. In *The Prophetic Imagination* he calls it the "royal consciousness," the settled state of a people
findings.why: 'Carved over the door of every church' is manufactured intensity. 'In *Title* (YEAR) he ...' appears four times across the two political/doubt essays in the same shape.

findings.quote: And the prophet — Samuel here, Amos later, Jesus finally — exists to break the spell and remind the people that they chose this, that the throne they begged for is the throne that is eating them.
findings.replacement: And the prophet (Samuel here, Amos later, Jesus finally) exists to remind the people that they chose this, and that the throne they begged for is the one now taking from them.
findings.why: Em-dash pair, plus 'break the spell' and 'eating them' where the chapter's own verb, take, is plainer and stronger.

findings.quote: ## Fear is the factory where false theology is made
findings.replacement: ## How fear changes what a church believes
findings.why: Headings are plain and descriptive; this one is an epigram.

findings.quote: Here is the engine under all of it, and it is not politics. It is fear, and fear has a way of rewriting your doctrine without telling you.
findings.replacement: Underneath all of it is fear, more than politics, and fear has a way of rewriting your doctrine without telling you.
findings.why: 'Here is the ...' is a stock AI turn, joined to an 'it is not X. It is Y.'

findings.quote: he argued that human groups — nations, tribes, churches as voting blocs — are far more selfish
findings.replacement: he argued that human groups (nations, tribes, churches as voting blocs) are far more selfish
findings.why: Em-dash.

findings.quote: Niebuhr's warning was that anxiety is the raw material of idolatry — that the most dangerous thing about a frightened people is not what it fears but what it will worship to feel safe.
findings.replacement: Niebuhr's warning was that anxiety is the raw material of idolatry, and that the most dangerous thing about a frightened people is what it will worship to feel safe.
findings.why: Em-dash and another not-X-but-Y. Also see for_james: anxiety as the ground of sin is Niebuhr's argument in The Nature and Destiny of Man, not in Moral Man and Immoral Society.

findings.quote: This is the part I refuse to wave away, because the people reaching for the strongman are not fools.
findings.replacement: The people reaching for the strongman are not fools.
findings.why: He does the fair thing; he doesn't announce that he is doing it.

findings.quote: They are not imagining the threat. The threat has a return address.
findings.replacement: They are not imagining the threat.
findings.why: A clever tag on a sentence that had already landed.

findings.quote: he is not speaking to nothing. He is speaking to a real wound, and that is precisely why the temptation is so strong. **The strongman never wins by lying about the danger. He wins by telling the truth about the danger and then offering himself as the only salvation from it.**
findings.replacement: he is speaking to a real wound, and that is why the temptation is so strong. The strongman doesn't have to lie about the danger. He tells the truth about it and then offers himself as the only salvation from it.
findings.why: Two 'not X. Y.' pairs back to back, the second in bold. One verdict line per essay is in bold already (paragraph two).

findings.tell: imperative signpost; double antithesis; em-dash pair
findings.quote: Read what the third temptation actually is. It is not a temptation to sin in some petty way. It is the offer of real power for a real purpose — all the kingdoms, all the power to set the world right — at the price of one act of worship. The devil does not tempt Jesus with weakness. He tempts him with *effectiveness.*
findings.replacement: The third temptation is no petty sin. It is the offer of real power for a real purpose, all the kingdoms and all the power to set the world right, at the price of one act of worship. The devil tempts Jesus with *effectiveness.*
findings.why: Four machine habits in five sentences.

findings.quote: says no — because the whole gospel hangs on the refusal to be that kind of king.
findings.replacement: says no, because the whole gospel hangs on his refusal to be that kind of king.
findings.why: Em-dash.

findings.quote: We are not the first church to face this, and the last church that faced it left us a warning written in its own ruin.
findings.replacement: We are not the first church to face this. The German church faced it in 1933 and left us a warning.
findings.why: 'The last church that faced it' is not true as history, and 'written in its own ruin' is ornament.

findings.quote: on what the German word *Führer* — leader — actually means,
findings.replacement: on what the German word *Führer*, leader, actually means,
findings.why: Em-dash pair.

findings.quote: will inevitably become a *Verführer* — a misleader, a seducer.
findings.replacement: will inevitably become a *Verführer*, a misleader, a seducer.
findings.why: Em-dash.

findings.quote: He had named, in the first week, the thing that would take a nation a decade and a continent of graves to confirm.
findings.replacement: He had named in the first week what the next decade would confirm.
findings.why: 'A continent of graves' is written for effect. The plain version carries more grief.

findings.quote: The danger is not only the strongman. The danger is the people who *want* one — the frightened crowd whose hunger to be saved by a man creates the very vacuum the man rushes to fill.
findings.replacement: The danger is also the people who *want* a strongman, the frightened crowd whose hunger to be saved by a man creates the very vacuum the man rushes to fill.
findings.why: The same paragraph also has 'Germany did not fall because ... Germany fell because ...'. Keep that one; it is the hinge.

findings.quote: I have sat across from the fear. I know it is not stupid, and I will not insult the people who carry it by pretending it is. But I have also read what the fear built, both in Ramah and in Berlin, and the record is not ambiguous.
findings.replacement: I have sat across from this fear, and it isn't stupid. But I have also read what the fear built, both in Ramah and in Berlin.
findings.why: 'The record is not ambiguous' is the stamp the brief lists ('the record', 'the verdict is not close'), and 'I will not insult ...' announces his own fairness.

findings.quote: The answer is the hardest one, because it is not a strategy. It is a different object of trust.
findings.replacement: The answer is hard because it comes down to whom we trust, and no strategy can stand in for that.
findings.why: Another 'it is not X. It is Y.', and 'object of trust' is seminar language.

findings.quote: when your God seems too slow, too invisible, too unwilling to fight your battles on your timeline. And Isaiah calls running to Egypt what it is — not strategy, but a failure of faith dressed as prudence.
findings.replacement: when your God seems too slow and too invisible to fight your battles on your timeline. And Isaiah calls running to Egypt a failure of faith dressed as prudence.
findings.why: The third item is padding (too unwilling repeats too slow), and the close is the antithesis again.

findings.quote: Read the logic. The proof that his kingdom is not of this world is precisely that it does not fight the way this world fights. The absence of the chariots is the presence of the kingdom.
findings.replacement: The proof that his kingdom is not of this world is that it does not fight the way this world fights.
findings.why: 'The absence of X is the presence of Y' is the pillow line the brief names (chiasmus at a paragraph end).

findings.quote: And here is the verdict I cannot soften, because the story does not soften it. The strongman is not the enemy of the frightened church. The strongman is the *answer to its prayer.* That is what makes this so much worse than a political mistake.
findings.replacement: The story does not soften what comes next, so I won't either. The strongman is the *answer* to the frightened church's prayer, which makes this much worse than a political mistake.
findings.why: 'Verdict' is the editorial rule written into the prose, and the paragraph holds three antitheses. Keep only 'The judgment was not the king. The judgment was getting the king.'

findings.quote: And the deepest tragedy of 1 Samuel 8 is not that the people wanted a tyrant. It is that they wanted a protector so badly
findings.replacement: And the deepest tragedy of 1 Samuel 8 is that they wanted a protector so badly
findings.why: The essay's first line already said they did not ask for a tyrant.

findings.quote: I do not get to stand outside this, because the church I belong to is the church praying the prayer.
findings.replacement: The church I belong to is the church praying this prayer.
findings.why: He implicates himself by doing it, not by announcing it.

findings.quote: fight our battles — who will take, if he must, our integrity, our witness, our credibility with the very people we were sent to reach, so long as he wins. We have read the warning and we are paying the cost anyway, because fear does not do arithmetic.
findings.replacement: fight our battles, who will take, if he must, our integrity, our witness, our credibility with the very people we were sent to reach, so long as he wins. We have read the warning and we are paying the cost anyway.
findings.why: 'Fear does not do arithmetic' was good once, in section one. Repeated word for word it becomes a refrain.

findings.quote: We are telling ourselves it is responsibility. We are telling ourselves it is the only realistic option. We are telling ourselves that a frightened church reaching for a fist is just being prudent in a dangerous time.
findings.replacement: We tell ourselves it's responsibility, the only realistic option, simple prudence in a dangerous time.
findings.why: Third three-beat anaphora in the essay ('It arrives as', 'They have watched', 'They thought').

findings.quote: refusing to the last the kingdoms a strongman would have seized — and he won the only war that was ever actually at stake.
findings.replacement: refusing to the last the kingdoms a strongman would have seized, and he won the only war that was ever actually at stake.
findings.why: Em-dash.

findings.also_in: /home/user/Livewell-/client/src/lib/shelf.json (essays[] entry with slug strongman-theology, field blurb)
findings.tell: em-dash pair in the public blurb
findings.quote: A frightened church always asks for a king. Israel did it first — give us a king like the other nations — and a prophet told them exactly what fear would cost them. We are praying the same prayer.
findings.replacement: A frightened church asks for a king. Israel did it first, asking for a king like the other nations, and a prophet told them what fear would cost them. We are praying the same prayer.
findings.why: This line shows under the title on /writing. It is the first thing a reader sees.

findings.quote: the Lord — Samuel was not bluffing — does not always answer in that day.
findings.replacement: the Lord (Samuel was not bluffing) does not always answer in that day.
findings.why: Every remaining U+2014 in this file takes the same treatment: comma, parentheses, colon or a period. Lines 14, 22, 26, 32, 36, 42, 44, 46, 52, 54, 62, 64 of the file each hold at least one.

findings.tell: search-engine language in the prose; em-dash; 'honest' as self-certifying; personification closer
findings.quote: and it is the question that drives people to the search bar at two in the morning — why am I afraid of God, why does the faith that was supposed to free me feel like a hand at my throat. The honest answer is that fear got into the foundations, and it did not knock.
findings.replacement: and it is the question people ask at two in the morning: why am I afraid of God, and why does the faith that was supposed to free me feel like a hand at my throat? The answer is that fear got into the foundations.
findings.why: The SEO brief is showing through the essay. No person writing to a frightened friend mentions the search bar.

findings.quote: And you can watch the same thing happen at the scale of a whole culture, which is why the search query keeps changing form but never disappears.
findings.replacement: And you can watch the same thing happen at the scale of a whole culture.
findings.why: Same leak as F01.

findings.quote: But fear has a counterfeit even here, and this is where the search for honest answers gets hard.
findings.replacement: But fear has a counterfeit even here.
findings.why: Third appearance of the search motif; 'honest' is used four times as a self-certifying adjective in this piece.

findings.quote: Consider the machinery before you blame the soul.
findings.replacement: Before you blame your soul, look at what fear does to a mind.
findings.why: 'Consider ...' is on the brief's stamp list, and the line is an epigram doing a signpost's job.

findings.tell: pop neuroscience stated as fact; literary image
findings.quote: Fear narrows. That is its whole job. The amygdala does not write essays; it sounds an alarm and shuts down the slow rooms of the brain where reflection lives, the rooms where you weigh, qualify, hold two things at once.
findings.replacement: Fear narrows. It sounds an alarm and crowds out the slower thinking where you weigh, qualify, and hold two things at once.
findings.why: A brain-anatomy claim with no source in a piece read by anxious people, and 'the slow rooms of the brain' is the fresh literary image the brief warns against.

findings.quote: Jonathan Haidt, in *The Righteous Mind* (2012), describes the rider and the elephant — the small rational rider
findings.replacement: Jonathan Haidt, in *The Righteous Mind*, describes the rider and the elephant: the small rational rider
findings.why: Em-dash; the year does no work.

findings.quote: The theology is real. It just isn't reasoned. It is the alarm, given vocabulary.
findings.replacement: The theology is real. It just isn't reasoned.
findings.why: Nearly every paragraph in this essay ends on an epigram. See pattern P3.

findings.quote: Not through study. Through dread.
findings.replacement: They get there through dread, not study.
findings.why: Fragment stack.

findings.quote: Neither of them argued their way there. They were carried there by a feeling that learned to talk.
findings.replacement: Neither of them argued their way there.
findings.why: 'A feeling that learned to talk' and, later, 'panic that learned to stand up straight' are the same manufactured line.

findings.quote: Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* (2007), describes the modern condition as the loss of a world we could take for granted — the buffered self standing alone
findings.replacement: Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age*, describes the modern condition as the loss of a world we could take for granted: the buffered self standing alone
findings.why: Em-dash; third 'X, in *Title* (YEAR), describes' in the piece.

findings.tell: bold slogan; antithesis; two pillow closers in a row
findings.quote: **A church that is afraid does not preach the kingdom. It preaches the bunker.** It draws the line tighter, names the enemy faster, mistakes its own anxiety for the holiness of God. The fortress feels like faithfulness. It is fear with a steeple.
findings.replacement: A church that is afraid stops preaching the kingdom and starts preaching the bunker. It draws the line tighter, names the enemy faster, and mistakes its own anxiety for the holiness of God.
findings.why: 'It is fear with a steeple' is the line most likely to make a careful reader say a machine wrote this.

findings.quote: ## I have preached the bunker
findings.replacement: ## Fear in the pulpit
findings.why: The heading and the paragraph under it ('There were seasons when I read the headlines before I read the Psalms ... I taught a frightened God to a frightened room') are a first-person confession nobody has confirmed. If James says it happened, keep the paragraph. If not, it must go. See for_james.

findings.quote: I want to be precise about this, because it is easy to write these sentences as though the failure belongs to other pastors, the loud ones, the ones on television. It does not.
findings.replacement: It would be easy to write this as though the failure belongs to other pastors, the loud ones, the ones on television. It doesn't.
findings.why: The prose is describing its own method.

findings.tell: epigram signpost; em-dash pair; tidy triplet
findings.quote: This is the trap inside the trap. The frightened God is useful. He gives you something to do with the dread. He turns the formless three-in-the-morning terror into a project — a doctrine to guard, a boundary to police, an enemy to name — and the project is so absorbing that you never notice you have stopped worshiping and started bracing.
findings.replacement: The frightened God is useful. He gives you something to do with the dread. He turns the formless three-in-the-morning terror into a project, a doctrine to guard or an enemy to name, and the project is so absorbing that you never notice you've stopped worshiping and started bracing.
findings.why: The same three items were listed two sentences earlier ('what to defend and whom to suspect').

findings.quote: ## The fear that heals and the fear that hides
findings.replacement: ## Two kinds of fear
findings.why: Alliterative, symmetrical heading.

findings.tell: statistic that cannot be verified; overclaim
findings.quote:
The most repeated command in the book is aimed straight at it.

Three hundred times, give or take, the line returns.
findings.replacement:
One of the most repeated commands in the book is aimed straight at it.

Again and again the line returns.
findings.why: The '300 (or 365) fear nots' figure is a pulpit commonplace that does not survive a count. A skeptic who checks it stops trusting everything around it.

findings.quote: If you wanted the one sentence God says more than any other to human beings, that is the sentence, and the frequency is the revelation.
findings.replacement: If you wanted one sentence God keeps saying to human beings, that is the sentence.
findings.why: Follows from F16; 'the frequency is the revelation' is a slogan.

findings.quote: You can test your theology against this, and the test is brutally simple.
findings.replacement: You can test your theology against this.
findings.why: 'Brutally simple' is intensity with nothing behind it.

findings.tell: Scripture not verbatim and without reference
findings.quote: *I heard you in the garden, and I was afraid, so I hid.* God was not hunting him. God was walking in the cool of the day, calling his name, asking the only question fear cannot answer — *where are you*.
findings.replacement: *I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself* (Genesis 3:10). God was not hunting him. God was walking in the cool of the day, calling to him, asking the one question fear cannot answer: *Where are you?* (Genesis 3:9).
findings.why: Italic lines read as quotation; site rule is ESV verbatim with the reference. The text says God called to the man; it does not say he called his name. Applier: check both verses against the ESV.

findings.quote: The hiding was the theology. Adam met grace and read it as a manhunt, because fear had gotten there first and recolored the whole face of God.
findings.replacement: Adam met grace and read it as a manhunt, because fear had gotten there first.
findings.why: 'The hiding was the theology' and, two paragraphs on, 'The bracing is the theology' are one stamped formula.

findings.tell: Scripture not verbatim and without reference; literary image
findings.quote: *Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment.* John writes it plainly in his first letter, and we read it as a greeting card, and we miss the surgery in it.
findings.replacement: *There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment* (1 John 4:18). We read it like a greeting card and miss what John is doing.
findings.why: ESV verbatim with the reference; 'the surgery in it' is ornament.

findings.tell: antithesis; literary image; bold slogan; stamped formula
findings.quote: John is not being sentimental; he is naming a mechanism. Fear is what runs the soul that expects to be punished, and a soul that expects punishment will build a punishing God to match, because the architecture of the inner life always projects itself onto the ceiling. We do not see God as he is. **We see God as we are braced for him to be.** And the bracing is the theology. The bracing is what we defend on Sunday,
findings.replacement: John is naming a mechanism. Fear is what runs the soul that expects to be punished, and a soul that expects punishment will build a punishing God to match. We see God as we are braced for him to be, and the bracing is what we defend on Sunday,
findings.why: Keep 'We see God as we are braced for him to be' as the essay's one earned line, without the bold and without the scaffolding around it.

findings.quote: Walter Brueggemann spent a career insisting that the Psalms refuse to lie about fear, and that the refusal is the recovery. In *The Message of the Psalms* (1984) he traced the movement from orientation through disorientation to a new orientation, and he warned against the thing the frightened church does instinctively — skipping the middle.
findings.replacement: Walter Brueggemann, in *The Message of the Psalms*, traced the movement from orientation through disorientation to a new orientation. The frightened church instinctively skips the middle.
findings.why: 'Spent a career insisting' and 'he warned against' put words in his mouth. Keep what the book actually does and let the application be James's own.

findings.quote: It is faith dragging the fear into the light where it can finally be seen for what it is — a feeling and not a fact, a weather system and not the face of God. A church that cannot pray the frightened Psalms out loud will preach a frightened God by accident, every single time, because the fear it would not speak does not leave. It just changes pulpits.
findings.replacement: It is faith dragging the fear into the light, where it can be seen as a feeling and not the face of God. A church that cannot pray the frightened Psalms out loud will preach a frightened God by accident, because the fear it would not speak does not leave.
findings.why: 'It just changes pulpits' is a kicker; 'every single time' is filler intensity.

findings.quote: So how does it get undone. Not by trying harder to be brave. Bravery is another thing fear can fake; a clenched jaw is not a quiet heart, and white-knuckled certainty is just panic that learned to stand up straight.
findings.replacement: So how does it get undone? Trying harder to be brave won't do it. Bravery is another thing fear can fake, and a clenched jaw is not a quiet heart.
findings.why: Three epigrams where one would do.

findings.tell: em-dash; joke epigram in a crisis-facing passage
findings.quote: refusing to let it keep its disguise as discernment — refusing to dignify the three-in-the-morning dread with the word *wisdom* when it is only adrenaline with a theology degree.
findings.replacement: refusing to let it keep its disguise as discernment, refusing to call the three-in-the-morning dread *wisdom*.
findings.why: 'Adrenaline with a theology degree' is a quip aimed at a reader who may be in real distress.

findings.tell: crisis-facing passage with no path to help
findings.quote: because you will be the last to see it; the rewriting is invisible from inside the rewritten mind.
findings.replacement: because you will be the last to see it; the rewriting is invisible from inside the rewritten mind. If the dread has become more than you can carry, tell a pastor, a doctor or a counselor, and start with [Find Help](/help). In the US you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any hour.
findings.why: The piece names three-in-the-morning terror, a hand at the throat and scrupulosity (in its keywords) and never points to help. The brief requires the link. This is the one addition recommended; nothing else in this audit adds content.

findings.quote: It still comes — Jesus sweat blood in a garden, so do not tell me the goal is never to feel it — but it no longer writes the doctrine.
findings.replacement: It still comes. Jesus sweat blood in a garden, so the goal can't be never to feel it. But it no longer writes the doctrine.
findings.why: Em-dash pair.

findings.tell: 'honest' as self-certifying adjective; fragment antithesis; epigram
findings.quote: Not a performance of certainty, which is only fear in costume. A confession that the dread has gotten into the foundations,
findings.replacement: It is a confession that the dread has gotten into the foundations,
findings.why: 'Fear in costume' is the fifth version of the same disguise image (clothes of conviction, dress itself as discernment, disguise as discernment, fear with a steeple).

findings.quote: The honest prayer in all of this is old and short.
findings.replacement: The prayer for all of this is old and short.
findings.why: Fourth 'honest'.

findings.tell: clever-kicker ending; antithesis; unsafe for a scrupulous reader
findings.quote: Look hard at the God you are most certain of when you are most afraid. That is not God. That is the elephant, explained.
findings.replacement: Look hard at the God you are most certain of when you are most afraid, and ask whether he is the one who keeps saying, *Do not be afraid.*
findings.why: The essay ends on a callback to a psychology metaphor instead of on Christ or Scripture, and 'That is not God' is a flat verdict on the faith of a frightened reader. The replacement uses only what the essay already established.

findings.tell: biography used as a credential; literary phrasing
findings.quote: I came to faith out of atheism, which means I know what it is to build a god out of nothing and call it nature, to assemble a universe with no one home in it and learn to live in the cold of that.
findings.replacement: I came to faith out of atheism, so I know what it is to live in a universe with no one home in it.
